newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope urges communist China to legalise Church. [CORRECTED 15:53 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Pope urges communist China to legalise Church. [CORRECTED 15:53 GMT]

text.p: Pope John Paul made a public appeal to China's communist government on Tuesday to legalise the Roman Catholic Church and allow members to worship openly.
"Let the civil authorities of the People's Republic of China be reassured," the Pope said in a message he read at a special mass broadcast by radio to Asia.
"A disciple of Christ can live his own faith in any political order, as long as his right is respected to behave according to the dictates of his conscience and of his own faith," he said.
Urging China's government not to "be afraid either of God or his Church", he added:

"I therefore ask them, with a sense of deference, to respect the authentic freedom which is the birthright of every man and woman and to allow believers in Christ to be able to contribute their energies and talents to the development of the nation.
"The Chinese nation has an important role to play in the bosom of the community of nations. Catholics can lend significant support to that and they will do so with enthusiasm and dedication."
Catholics in China are allowed to worship openly only if they belong to the state-sponsored Catholic Patriotic Association.

The association appoints its own bishops and does not recognise the Pope's authority. The official Catholic Church in China counts four million members, while the underground church is believed to have several million members.

The Pope was speaking at a Vatican mass held to mark the 70th anniversary of the ordination of the first Chinese bishops in Rome in 1926 and the 50th anniversary of the establishment of a Roman Catholic Church hierarchy in China in 1946.
The Vatican said the service was broadcast live by Vatican radio and the Philippines-based station Radio Veritas (corrects from Radio Manila).

The Pope urged Catholics in China to remain faithful to Rome and not "yield to conceptions of a Church which do not correspond to the will of the Lord Jesus, to the Catholic faith, or to the sentiments and convictions of the great majority of Chinese Catholics.
"I urge all pastors and faithful in China to express with courage, and without fear, the true profession of Catholic faith," the Pope said.
He also urged bishops of the underground church to seek reconciliation with the official church, on the basis of union with Rome, and said he hoped one day to visit China.
The official church, which recently ordained about 50 new priests, has the blessing of the Chinese Communist Party.
The Washington-based rights group Human Rights Watch/Asia has said Beijing has been stepping up harassment of unauthorised Catholic and Protestant groups in recent years.
Vatican relations with Beijing have alternately cooled and warmed over the decades since the late 1950s, when links were severed over the Vatican's recognition of Taiwan.
China has said it will not normalise ties until the Vatican severs its links with Taiwan, which Beijing has regarded as a rebel province since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
The Vatican has demanded recognition of the Pope's primacy before it renews ties with China.
